title: From Laptop to Cluster: The Agentic AI Inner Loop on Kubernetes
tldr: Using a live audience race game run by an AI race director, the speaker shows an agentic Java app built with Quarkus and LangChain4j that exposes MCP tools and calls sub-agents over A2A. He argues agents are mostly ordinary code: develop locally with hot reload and a dev UI, add evals, then ship to Kubernetes with configuration changes and standard security and health patterns.

key_points.text: Gartner research cited: many agentic AI projects will be canceled because of rising costs, unclear business value and weak risk controls.
The demo game sends phone taps through Kafka to a dashboard, with an AI race director that monitors the race, changes themes and boosts teams that fall behind, with human approval.
The game exposes MCP servers; the admin server requires browser authentication so not every user or agent can control the game.
The race director is a supervisor agent that picks between an analyst and a creative sub-agent over A2A, similar to distributed services owned by different teams.
MCP and A2A act like a new REST: MCP tools are annotated Java methods with role-based access, such as admin-only tools.
An open-source tool can turn existing APIs into MCP servers by configuration, without rewriting them.
Quarkus dev mode gives hot reload, a dev UI listing Kafka topics, AI services, MCP tools, prompt templates and token metrics, and exposes runtime info to the code assistant over MCP.
Local development still enforces the same MCP authentication, so you test production auth on your laptop.
Swapping models changes behavior: a boost prompt produced a 1.5 multiplier on one model and 3 on another, so add evals to the test suite.
For production: switch models via configuration, add health checks for sub-agents and MCP servers, expose token and latency metrics, use mutual TLS and short-lived tokens (SPIFFE/SPIRE, Keycloak).

numbers.text: Gartner expects more than 40% of agentic AI projects to be canceled by the end of next year.
The same boost prompt gave a 1.5 multiplier on the original model and 3 on a new one.

open_gaps.text: Agentic apps with many components are hard to test, and a race director and code assistant can conflict over the same controls.
Changing models can silently change agent behavior unless prompts are detailed and evals cover it.
Agents need guardrails, sandboxing and least-privilege, short-lived credentials when they run in Kubernetes.

opportunities.text: Add evals for non-deterministic agent behavior to your test suite with tools like Langfuse or Promptfoo.
Add health endpoints that check A2A sub-agents and MCP servers, not just the main app.
Try the game's source on GitHub to see MCP tools with role-based access and an A2A supervisor agent in Java.
Join the CNCF developer experience TAG, which the speaker says is looking for contributors.
